title: Infrared Memory of a Majorana Shutter
abstract: We study a finite-width Majorana shutter as a local, time-dependent scattering defect and determine which features of its infrared memory are insensitive to the microscopic spatial profile. For a smooth shutter, the zero-frequency scattering matrix is fixed by the integrated coupling, while finite-width corrections vanish in the long-wavelength limit. A time-dependent switch then produces an infrared Bogoliubov kernel whose singular part is controlled by the change in this scattering matrix.   We examine the many-body response through three observables. The overlap of the pre- and post-shutter Gaussian vacua exhibits Anderson orthogonality, with an exponent set by the scattering angle. A lattice calculation of the post-quench quasiparticle number resolves its logarithmic infrared growth, reaching the predicted coefficient in the slow-switch test and reproducing the expected dependence on the scattering-angle change. When the entanglement cut passes through the shutter, the entropy follows the effective-central-charge description of a conformal defect, with parameter-free agreement at the percent level, improving for the wider shutter. When the shutter lies inside the interval, its contribution remains a subleading finite-size correction. A local bilinear correlator approaches the expected Majorana power law and shows no stable logarithmic amplitude.   These results show that the same low-frequency scattering data control distinct global and spatial observables, while their infrared coefficients are not interchangeable. The remaining limits are also made explicit: the finite-memory correction to the continuum kernel and the controlled continuum limit of large-interval spatial entropy.
summary: This work analyzes the 'infrared memory' left in a fermionic system by a localized, time-varying defect (Majorana shutter). By examining multiple observables—including entanglement entropy and quasiparticle number—the authors demonstrate that the low-frequency physics is governed by distinct coefficients, proving that global and local measures of quantum memory are not mathematically equivalent.
main_problem: The study investigates the 'infrared memory' imprinted on a quantum system by a local, time-dependent scattering defect modeled as a Majorana shutter.
main_result: The analysis establishes that global infrared divergences (like in quasiparticle number) and local spatial entropy divergences are controlled by distinct, though related, low-frequency scattering data, showing they are not interchangeable.
method: The authors use analytical techniques involving the scattering matrix, Bogoliubov kernels, and lattice simulations to probe the system's response to time-dependent perturbations.
model_or_system: The system is a 1D fermionic chain described by massless Majorana fields, perturbed by a smooth, finite-width coupling acting as the 'Majorana shutter' defect.
key_observables: Overlap of Gaussian vacua (Anderson orthogonality), post-quench quasiparticle number (logarithmic growth), and entanglement entropy (central-charge description).
important_parameters: The finite width ($a$) and the switching time ($	au$) define the memory parameter ($\epsilon_{	ext{mem}} = a/	au$), and the scattering angle ($	heta_\lambda$) controls the zero-frequency scattering matrix.
main_assumptions: The analysis often relies on the zero-memory approximation ($\epsilon_{	ext{mem}} \ll 1$) and treats the system using continuum field theory methods.
figures_summary: The notes do not provide a summary of figures, but they detail the quantitative results for various observables like the overlap exponent, the logarithmic coefficient, and the entropy scaling.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the universality of the zero-frequency scattering matrix, then analyzing the time-dependent Bogoliubov kernel, and finally comparing the resulting divergences across global (quasiparticle number) and local (entropy) observables.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous framework for distinguishing between different types of quantum memory effects—global vs. local—in strongly correlated, non-equilibrium fermionic systems, which is crucial for understanding quantum quenches.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Ground-state overlap as a finite-size BCC/orthogonality diagnostic at λf = 0.4, a = 2. The lattice data for three smooth profiles follow a common power law. The dashed line uses the parameter-free infrared prediction γAO = (∆θ/2π)2. Profile dependence is visible only at the finite-size level and is substantially smaller than the leading power-law scaling signal.

Figure 2: Extracted orthogonality exponent versus the scattering prediction γAO = (∆θ/2π)2. The numerical exponent is obtained from finite-size ground-state overlaps. The diagonal line is not a fit; it is the analytic scattering prediction.

Figure 3: Loschmidt amplitude after a sudden switch for N = 512, a = 2, w1, and λf = 0.4. The pre-revival data give slopes in the range 0.00773–0.00804 for the fit windows listed in the text, compared with 2γAO = 0.007695. The late-time deviation is a finite-size recurrence effect, not an LCFT signature.

Figure 4: Vacuum control for the connected bulk bilinear exponent. The fits use the anchored two-component form Ar−p + (−1)rBr−q with j = N/2 and 5 ≤r ≤min(102, N/4). The finite-size drift toward p = 2 is already present at λf = 0; the shutter changes the fitted exponent only weakly.

Figure 5: Direct logarithmic-partner diagnostic using the correct log(r/aUV) ansatz. At N = 512, Blog/A is −8 × 10−8 in the vacuum and 7 × 10−6 at λf = 0.4. The small, regulator-dependent amplitudes do not establish a logarithmic two-point function.
